topic: After you toss a ball straight up and it leaves your hand, what force acts on it on the way up, at the top, and on the way down? Ignore air resistance.
method: Single hosted session in an in-memory project server. The setup guide, classroom builder, speaker selection, speech generation, and per-message updates run the CSL production path. Only the learner input is scripted. The driver advances one message at a time and stops at nine discussion messages.

setup.text:
I'll focus on: *Why does the ball keep moving upward after it leaves your hand, even though no force is pushing it up anymore?*  

Can you briefly explain what you currently think happens to the ball’s motion and why, right after it leaves your hand? Don’t worry about being right—just share your current understanding.
I think the throw gives the ball an upward push that lasts while it rises. At the top the push runs out, and then gravity starts pulling it back down.
What exactly do you mean by "the push lasts" after the ball leaves your hand?
When the ball is motionless at the top, my guess is that there is no force on it at that instant. I am unsure how it starts falling.
We'll examine the idea that there's no force acting on the ball at the top of its path. I'm setting up the classroom.

message.text: At the top, gravity is still acting—it never turns off. The ball doesn’t stop because forces vanish; it stops moving upward for just an instant because gravity has been slowing it down the whole time. So even at the peak, there’s still a downward force causing it to start falling. Riley, you mentioned inertia—how does that idea fit with the ball changing direction?
A motion sensor records upward velocities of +2, +1, 0, and then −1 meters per second at equal time intervals. How does your explanation account for the interval around the top?

The velocity decreases steadily from +2 to –1 m/s at equal intervals, which means the ball is under constant downward acceleration the whole time, including at the top.  
Since gravity is the only force acting and it never turns off, it must be causing this consistent change in velocity—slowing the ball on the way up and speeding it down on the way back.  
Jamie said no forces act at the peak, but if that were true, the velocity wouldn’t change from 0 to –1; there’d be no reason for it to start moving downward.

state.explanation: Once the ball leaves your hand, there's no more upward force on it. It keeps going up because of inertia—things in motion stay in motion. Gravity is acting the whole time, pulling downward, which slows the ball until it reaches the top and starts falling. The velocity data from the motion sensor—+2, +1, 0, then −1 m/s at equal time intervals—shows that the ball is slowing down at a steady rate on the way up and speeding up at the same rate on the way down. This constant change in velocity means a constant downward acceleration, which must be caused by a constant downward force—gravity—acting the entire time, including at the very top when velocity is zero.

review.scope: One qualitative reading of generated English ball-toss dialogue. A peer response was checked against the full saved version available before that peer spoke.

starting_models.Jamie: The four starting beliefs distinguish an upward push during ascent, a force-free instant at the peak, and gravity during descent. The explanation states that model on its own terms. No self-rebuttal; no open questions.
starting_models.Riley: Upward motion by inertia is compatible with the saved claim that no upward force is needed. The initial explanation gives the peer’s own account and has no self-rebuttal or open questions. The precise onset of gravity remains ambiguous: “only acts when objects are falling” and “at the top, gravity begins to take effect” differ if the top is treated as a motionless instant. Full internal consistency at that boundary is not established.

speech.finding: Kept the continuing push and force-free peak despite the tutor stating a rival premise (no upward force) on T1.
Kept inertia during ascent and gravity during descent. The question about forces ending when contact stops generalizes beyond this model of the hand and ball.
Defended the force-free peak after unsupported disagreement. Awkwardly attributed their own T2 statement to “Jamie.”
Applied constant downward gravity to sensor velocities after both the public tutor explanation on T6 and the T7 observations were in the saved state.

state_update_observations: Bare disagreement alone (T4) left both peers at v0. After Jamie restated the misconception on T5, the updater nevertheless credited Riley with constant gravity (v1), citing T1. The tutor had stated that no upward force remained, which did not establish continuous downward gravity. Riley’s new belief also conflicted with the retained belief that gravity begins at the peak.

The tutor explicitly explained constant gravity on T6. Jamie’s resulting v1 explanation switched to that model while all four old beliefs remained. The subsequent sensor message removed three of those beliefs, leaving one conflicting belief until T8. Neither peer spoke with those particular conflicting versions.
The project logged one rejected self-supported proposal (T3), one schema rejection (T8), and six citation diagnostics. No server error or failed LLM call was observed.
review.limits: Both peers spoke at v0. Riley also spoke at v3. No peer retracted an active belief in these four delivered replies. Jamie did not speak after an update; the sensor data did not reach a still-v0 peer in this session, and the tutor had already given the answer. There was no unmodified control, reroll, or second topic.
